questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how to model a run of consecutive integers
questions.stem: Memo lines for the school catchment list three consecutive house numbers whose sum is 132. A parent asks how to write the three numbers using one letter. Explain the method and how to find the smallest.

answer.exemplar: Three consecutive integers can be written as n, n plus 1 and n plus 2, and their sum is 3n plus 3. Setting that equal to 132 gives 3n equals 129, so the smallest is n equals 43, and the three house numbers are 43, 44 and 45. The method works because the three values are locked together with a fixed difference of 1, so one letter and one extra step describe the whole run. The trap is to write the numbers as n, n plus 1 and n plus 2 but then forget the 3 in front of n when adding them, which silently shifts every number up by one.

questions.explanation: Writing the numbers as n, n plus 1 and n plus 2 makes the sum 3n plus 3, so n equals 43 and the run is 43, 44 and 45. Forgetting the coefficient 3 is the common slip.
questions.hint: Write the run first, then add the three terms carefully.

questions.topic: A single point on a line
questions.learningObjective: explain how a point is tested against a line
questions.stem: A survey memo pins down the boundary path as the line y equals one half x plus 4, and records the point (6, 7). Explain how the memo decides whether that point is on the path.

answer.exemplar: To test a point against a line, the memo substitutes the x value for the x in the equation and works out the y value the line predicts, then compares it with the y value of the point. Here one half of 6 is 3, and 3 plus 4 is 7, which matches the recorded y value, so the point lies on the path. A point is a member of a line exactly when this substitution is exact, and the reason the test works is that the equation describes every point on the line and no others. Near misses are the danger, because a point one unit away still looks like it belongs when a memo is read quickly.

questions.explanation: The memo substitutes x equals 6 to get 3 plus 4, which is 7, the point's y value, so the point is on the path. A point lies on a line when the substitution is exact, and near misses are the danger.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why back-substitution is the strongest check
questions.stem: A memo on the allotment path rearranges 4x plus 6 equals 30 into x equals 6. Explain why back-substitution is the strongest way to confirm this.

answer.exemplar: Back-substitution replaces the answer in the original equation and checks that the original right-hand side comes back unchanged, which is exactly what a planner needs to know, because the original equation is the statement that came from the site rather than from the algebra. Here 4 times 6 plus 6 gives 30, the value the memo started from, so the rearrangement preserved the solution. The alternative checks are weaker: a check that repeats the same steps only shows the arithmetic was done consistently, and a check on the shape of the answer can be satisfied by a wrong value. What back-substitution adds is independence from the working, since it uses the original equation and the candidate alone.

questions.explanation: Putting x equals 6 back into 4x plus 6 gives 30, the memo's starting value, so the rearrangement preserved the solution. It uses the original equation, not the working, so slips stay visible.
questions.hint: The original equation should give back its right-hand side.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a graph and the algebra agree
questions.stem: A modelling memo plots two lines, y equals x plus 3 and y equals minus 2x plus 9, and asks for the meeting point. Explain how the graph and the algebra agree.

answer.exemplar: The meeting point is the single pair of coordinates that satisfies both rules at once, and because each rule gives one y value for any given x, that pair is found by setting the two rules equal. Here x plus 3 equals minus 2x plus 9, so 3x equals 6, x equals 2 and y equals 5. The graph and the algebra agree because the graph of a rule is nothing more than the list of its solutions drawn out, so the crossing of the two lines is the same point the equality produces. This matters in a memo, since a drawing alone shows roughly where two lines meet, and the algebra fixes the exact coordinates that a plan or a budget depends on.

questions.explanation: Setting x plus 3 equal to minus 2x plus 9 gives 3x equals 6, so x equals 2 and y equals 5, where the lines cross. The graph shows the crossing roughly, while the algebra fixes the exact coordinates.
questions.hint: The crossing point satisfies both rules at once.

answer.exemplar: The two rules have the same slope, 5, so they describe parallel lines, and parallel lines that are not the same line never meet. answer.exemplar: The second rule, y minus 2x equals 9, is the first rule rearranged, since subtracting 2x from both sides of y equals 2x plus 9 leaves exactly y minus 2x equals 9. Two rules that are algebraic restatements of one another describe a single line rather than two, so every point on that line satisfies both and the system has infinitely many solutions. This is different from a system with no solution, where the rules are parallel but distinct, because here the lines are not merely similar in slope, they are the same line. The check is to put the equations into the same form and compare the coefficients, and 2 and 9 here match exactly, which is what shows the two rules are one statement about the same set of points.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why an absolute value rule gives a range
questions.stem: A threshold memo sets a clearance rule: the absolute value of x minus 10 is less than 2. Explain why this gives a range rather than a single value.

answer.exemplar: The absolute value of x minus 10 is the distance between x and 10, so the rule says that distance must be under 2, which means x is greater than 8 and less than 12. The inequality is strict, so the endpoints 8 and 12 are excluded, while a rule using at most 2 would include them. The reason the result is a range rather than one number is that an absolute value rule never names a single point, it names a tolerance around a centre, and every point inside that tolerance satisfies it. That is why the same rule with an equality sign instead of an inequality would give exactly two points, 8 and 12, since both sit at distance 2 from the centre of 10.

questions.explanation: The absolute value of x minus 10 is the distance from 10, so the rule allows every x within 2 of 10, the range 8 to 12. A tolerance names a range, not a single point.
questions.hint: An absolute value measures a distance, so a range works.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a piecewise tariff is built
questions.stem: A charges memo gives a parking tariff of 3 dollars for the first hour and 1.5 dollars for each hour after that. Explain how the model is built and why it has two parts.

answer.exemplar: The tariff is built from two different rules because the price of parking does not rise in the way a single straight line would, since the first hour is a flat 3 dollars and only the hours beyond that are charged at 1.5 dollars each. For a stay of t hours with t greater than 1, the charge is 3 plus 1.5 times the number of hours after the first, that is 3 plus 1.5 times t minus 1, while for t less than or equal to 1 it is simply 3. The two parts matter because the second rate counts only the extra hours, and applying 1.5 dollars to the first hour as well would charge a customer for time already covered by the flat fee. A single formula would either overcharge short stays or undercharge long ones, which is why the planner wrote the model in two pieces with a stated range for each.

questions.explanation: The model has two parts because the first hour is a flat charge and only the hours beyond it are billed hourly. Applying 1.5 dollars to the first hour as well would overcharge a short stay.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the tariff each rule describes.

questions.learningObjective: explain the test for an arithmetic sequence
questions.stem: A survey memo lists 200 | 240 | 280 | 320 of new dwellings and asks how to tell whether the list is arithmetic. Explain the test and what it shows.

answer.exemplar: The test is to subtract each term from the term that follows it, and the list is arithmetic exactly when every one of those differences is the same. Here 240 minus 200 is 40, 280 minus 240 is 40, and 320 minus 280 is 40, so the common difference is 40 and the list is arithmetic. The same rule runs backwards, since 200 minus 240 is minus 40, which is how a planner predicts the next figure as 360 dwellings. What makes this a reliable test is that an arithmetic sequence is defined by a constant step, so a single gap that differs, such as 320 minus 280 being 50 instead of 40, would be enough to rule it out even if every other gap matched.
